doc.title: Catherine Russell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 26, 2018

title: Asserting herself with an arranger on her own record
summary: An arranger resisted a chord she wanted at a session; she insisted because her name was on the record.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Early on when you were making that transition, did you find that it was necessary to somehow let the accompanist, the band members, know that you know music? That you’re not a singer that was born with this great voice but doesn’t know about keys and doesn’t know about going to the bridge and all that. I mean I’m not sure I’m asking the question right. But have you felt like I have to let these players know that I’m informed.

It happens once in a while. So I would say when I was — no because this is like a two part answer. When I was working at the comedy club, Catch a Rising Star, I would have to come in and I’d sing three songs. So I was the one that brought them the charts. So if there was — so I’d write them up. You know I’d just write them up and give them to them and they would play them down and there was no question because I’d just say, “Here — okay no I meant a D minor there” or whatever. So people always know that I know what I want. I have had, though, because in the early days I didn’t have arrangers to work with because I wasn’t at that stage yet. So when I finally got to the stage where I needed arrangements, people were calling me and it was like, “I don’t have arrangements.” How do you get arrangements? You call an arranger and you pay them to arrange something for you. So there was one instance where the person, I had given that person the chord chart of the changes that I wanted and they decided not to do something that I wanted them to do, and held up my recording session saying — and I said, “No, at the end of the bridge there’s another chord there, that’s what I want.” And he said, “Well you send me the charts and I do what I want anyway.” I said, “Oh really? Okay I want that chord right there. So I’m going to wait until we get that chord in there because that’s what I want.” So I had to hold — I’m paying for everything and I had to hold up my session and he did his little bravado thing, and I just thought okay I’ll file that away. He’s

a fabulous arranger, I love what he does, but that was just one instance of having to stand up for myself and saying, “No, that’s what I want.” And he knows I know what I want but he was just exercising his — he figured I’ll put my own stamp on this. But I said no I’m putting my stamp on it because it’s — my name is on the record.
And it was just like one chord. That’s all. The same thing as a whole step down. Very easy to do.
